bank.module: Session 5 — Functions, Lambda & Advanced Function Concepts
bank.title: Python Session 5 — Production Bank 001

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Function Definition` according to the taught session?

options.text: A function is a reusable block of code defined to perform a specific task.
Parameters let a function receive values, and `return` sends a result back to the caller.
A default parameter provides a value used when the caller omits that argument.
A function can return multiple values that the caller can unpack into separate variables.

explanation.ar: A function is a reusable block of code defined to perform a specific task.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to define a reusable block of logic?

options.text: return
def function_name(...):
name="Guest"
q, r = divide(a, b)

explanation.ar: `def function_name(...):` is the course-aligned choice for this task: define a reusable block of logic.

questions.question: What is printed after `def greet(): print("Hello, world!")` followed by `greet()`?

options.text: greet
None only
Hello, world!
The function definition text

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `Function Definition` behavior: A function is a reusable block of code defined to perform a specific task.

questions.question: A learner writes statements intended for the function without indenting them under `def`. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `return` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Function Definition` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Default Parameters` without changing the logic.
Indent the function body under the `def` line.

explanation.ar: Indent the function body under the `def` line.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Parameters & Return` according to the taught session?

options.text: Parameters let a function receive values, and `return` sends a result back to the caller.
A default parameter provides a value used when the caller omits that argument.
A function can return multiple values that the caller can unpack into separate variables.
A docstring documents what a function does and can be read through the function `__doc__` attribute.

explanation.ar: Parameters let a function receive values, and `return` sends a result back to the caller.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to send a computed value back from a function?

options.text: name="Guest"
return
q, r = divide(a, b)
function.__doc__

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. `return` is the course-aligned choice for this task: send a computed value back from a function.

questions.question: What is the result of calling a taught `add(5, 3)` function that returns `a + b`?

options.text: None

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `Parameters & Return` behavior: Parameters let a function receive values, and `return` sends a result back to the caller.

questions.question: A learner prints a value inside a function and assumes that is identical to returning it to the caller. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `name="Guest"` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Parameters & Return` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Multiple Return Values` without changing the logic.
Use `return` when the caller needs the value as a result.

explanation.ar: Use `return` when the caller needs the value as a result.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Default Parameters` according to the taught session?

options.text: A default parameter provides a value used when the caller omits that argument.
A function can return multiple values that the caller can unpack into separate variables.
A docstring documents what a function does and can be read through the function `__doc__` attribute.
A lambda is a small anonymous function suited to short simple operations.

explanation.ar: A default parameter provides a value used when the caller omits that argument.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to provide a fallback argument value?

options.text: q, r = divide(a, b)
name="Guest"
function.__doc__
lambda x: ...

explanation.ar: `name="Guest"` is the course-aligned choice for this task: provide a fallback argument value.

questions.question: If `greet(name="Guest")` is called with no argument, which name is used?

options.text: None
name
Guest
An error always

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. The trace follows the taught `Default Parameters` behavior: A default parameter provides a value used when the caller omits that argument.

questions.question: A learner puts a non-default parameter after a default parameter in a way that breaks the intended signature. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `q, r = divide(a, b)` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Default Parameters` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Docstrings` without changing the logic.
Keep the function signature consistent with Python parameter rules and the taught default-value pattern.

explanation.ar: Keep the function signature consistent with Python parameter rules and the taught default-value pattern.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Multiple Return Values` according to the taught session?

options.text: A function can return multiple values that the caller can unpack into separate variables.
A docstring documents what a function does and can be read through the function `__doc__` attribute.
A lambda is a small anonymous function suited to short simple operations.
`map()` applies a function to each element of an iterable.

explanation.ar: A function can return multiple values that the caller can unpack into separate variables.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to unpack multiple returned values?

options.text: function.__doc__
q, r = divide(a, b)
lambda x: ...
map(function, iterable)

explanation.ar: `q, r = divide(a, b)` is the course-aligned choice for this task: unpack multiple returned values.

questions.question: The taught divide example returns quotient and remainder. What receives them?

options.text: One set only
A comment
Two variables such as q and r
A file object

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `Multiple Return Values` behavior: A function can return multiple values that the caller can unpack into separate variables.

questions.question: A learner expects two returned values but provides only one target variable while intending separate results. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `function.__doc__` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Multiple Return Values` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Lambda` without changing the logic.
Unpack the returned values into the corresponding variables.

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. Unpack the returned values into the corresponding variables.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Docstrings` according to the taught session?

options.text: A docstring documents what a function does and can be read through the function `__doc__` attribute.
A lambda is a small anonymous function suited to short simple operations.
`map()` applies a function to each element of an iterable.
`filter()` keeps iterable items for which the supplied function/condition is True.

explanation.ar: A docstring documents what a function does and can be read through the function `__doc__` attribute.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to read a function docstring?

options.text: lambda x: ...
function.__doc__
map(function, iterable)
filter(function, iterable)

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. `function.__doc__` is the course-aligned choice for this task: read a function docstring.

questions.question: Which attribute is shown for printing a function docstring?

options.text: __name__ only
append
__doc__
dtype

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `Docstrings` behavior: A docstring documents what a function does and can be read through the function `__doc__` attribute.

questions.question: A learner uses a normal output statement as if it were the function documentation metadata. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `lambda x: ...` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Docstrings` has no rules.
Convert the task to `map()` without changing the logic.
Place descriptive text as a docstring in the function and read it with `__doc__` when needed.

explanation.ar: Place descriptive text as a docstring in the function and read it with `__doc__` when needed.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Lambda` according to the taught session?

options.text: A lambda is a small anonymous function suited to short simple operations.
`map()` applies a function to each element of an iterable.
`filter()` keeps iterable items for which the supplied function/condition is True.
A recursive function calls itself on smaller subproblems and needs a stopping/base case.

explanation.ar: A lambda is a small anonymous function suited to short simple operations.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to define a short anonymous function?

options.text: map(function, iterable)
lambda x: ...
filter(function, iterable)
function calls itself

explanation.ar: `lambda x: ...` is the course-aligned choice for this task: define a short anonymous function.

questions.question: A taught lambda squares 5. What result is shown?

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. The trace follows the taught `Lambda` behavior: A lambda is a small anonymous function suited to short simple operations.

questions.question: A learner uses a large multi-step workflow inside a lambda and makes the code unreadable. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `map(function, iterable)` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Lambda` has no rules.
Convert the task to `filter()` without changing the logic.
Keep lambda usage for short simple operations; use a normal function for larger logic.

explanation.ar: Keep lambda usage for short simple operations; use a normal function for larger logic.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `map()` according to the taught session?

options.text: `map()` applies a function to each element of an iterable.
`filter()` keeps iterable items for which the supplied function/condition is True.
A recursive function calls itself on smaller subproblems and needs a stopping/base case.
A higher-order function can take another function as an argument or return a function.

explanation.ar: `map()` applies a function to each element of an iterable.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to apply one transformation to every item?

options.text: filter(function, iterable)
map(function, iterable)
function calls itself
function-as-argument / function-return

explanation.ar: `map(function, iterable)` is the course-aligned choice for this task: apply one transformation to every item.

questions.question: The taught square lambda mapped over `[1,2,3,4,5]` produces which list after conversion?

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `map()` behavior: `map()` applies a function to each element of an iterable.

questions.question: A learner expects `map()` by itself to display a ready list in every context. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `filter(function, iterable)` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `map()` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Recursion` without changing the logic.
Apply the function with `map()` and convert/consume the result as needed, as in the taught example.

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. Apply the function with `map()` and convert/consume the result as needed, as in the taught example.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `filter()` according to the taught session?

options.text: `filter()` keeps iterable items for which the supplied function/condition is True.
A recursive function calls itself on smaller subproblems and needs a stopping/base case.
A higher-order function can take another function as an argument or return a function.
A function is a reusable block of code defined to perform a specific task.

explanation.ar: `filter()` keeps iterable items for which the supplied function/condition is True.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to keep only items that satisfy a condition?

options.text: function calls itself
filter(function, iterable)
function-as-argument / function-return
def function_name(...):

explanation.ar: `filter(function, iterable)` is the course-aligned choice for this task: keep only items that satisfy a condition.

questions.question: The taught even-number filter on `[1,2,3,4,5,6]` keeps which values?

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `filter()` behavior: `filter()` keeps iterable items for which the supplied function/condition is True.

questions.question: A learner uses `filter()` when the goal is to transform every item rather than select items. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `function calls itself` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `filter()` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Higher-Order Functions` without changing the logic.
Use `filter()` for selection; use a transformation pattern such as `map()` when every item should be transformed.

explanation.ar: Use `filter()` for selection; use a transformation pattern such as `map()` when every item should be transformed.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Recursion` according to the taught session?

options.text: A recursive function calls itself on smaller subproblems and needs a stopping/base case.
A higher-order function can take another function as an argument or return a function.
A function is a reusable block of code defined to perform a specific task.
Parameters let a function receive values, and `return` sends a result back to the caller.

explanation.ar: A recursive function calls itself on smaller subproblems and needs a stopping/base case.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to solve a problem recursively with a base case?

options.text: function-as-argument / function-return
function calls itself
def function_name(...):
return

explanation.ar: `function calls itself` is the course-aligned choice for this task: solve a problem recursively with a base case.

questions.question: What result is taught for recursive factorial of 5?

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. The trace follows the taught `Recursion` behavior: A recursive function calls itself on smaller subproblems and needs a stopping/base case.

questions.question: A learner writes recursion without a reachable base case. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `function-as-argument / function-return` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Recursion` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Function Definition` without changing the logic.
Add a stopping/base case so recursive calls terminate.

explanation.ar: Add a stopping/base case so recursive calls terminate.

questions.question: Which statement best describes `Higher-Order Functions` according to the taught session?

options.text: A higher-order function can take another function as an argument or return a function.
A function is a reusable block of code defined to perform a specific task.
Parameters let a function receive values, and `return` sends a result back to the caller.
A default parameter provides a value used when the caller omits that argument.

explanation.ar: A higher-order function can take another function as an argument or return a function.

questions.question: Which taught function/pattern is most appropriate when you want to pass or return functions as values?

options.text: def function_name(...):
function-as-argument / function-return
return
name="Guest"

explanation.ar: `function-as-argument / function-return` is the course-aligned choice for this task: pass or return functions as values.

questions.question: In the taught `apply_operation(a,b,operation)` pattern, what is `operation`?

options.text: A list index
A file mode
A function passed as an argument
A NumPy shape

explanation.ar: The trace follows the taught `Higher-Order Functions` behavior: A higher-order function can take another function as an argument or return a function.

questions.question: A learner calls the operation before passing it when the design expects the function object itself. What correction best matches the course?

options.text: Use `def function_name(...):` instead regardless of the goal.
Ignore the issue because `Higher-Order Functions` has no rules.
Convert the task to `Parameters & Return` without changing the logic.
Pass the function object when the higher-order function is supposed to call it later.

explanation.ar: Platform clarification based on the taught concept. Pass the function object when the higher-order function is supposed to call it later.
